questions.q: Why is a number silently stored as text a dangerous problem in Excel?
options: It doesn't throw an error — it just quietly produces wrong SUM totals or failed lookups because Excel doesn't treat it as the same value as a real number
It always crashes the workbook immediately
Excel automatically deletes the cell
It only affects the cell's font color, nothing else
questions.explain: A text-formatted number causes no visible error — it just breaks aggregation and exact-match lookups silently, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

questions.q: Besides the green error triangle, what other visual tell identifies a number stored as text?
options: It left-aligns in the cell, instead of the normal right-alignment for numbers
It turns the cell red
It automatically adds a dollar sign
It shows a blue underline like a hyperlink
questions.explain: Numbers right-align by default and text left-aligns — this tell survives even if the green triangle error-checking feature is turned off.

questions.q: What does the VALUE() function do?
options: Converts a numeric-looking text string into a real number
Converts a real number into a formatted text label
Deletes all text from a cell
Rounds a number to the nearest integer
questions.explain: VALUE() takes text that looks like a number and converts it into an actual numeric value Excel can calculate with.

questions.q: What happens if you use DATEVALUE() on text that doesn't actually look like a date?
options: It returns a #VALUE! error, flagging the row for a human to check
It silently converts it to today's date
It converts it to the number zero with no warning
It deletes the entire row
questions.explain: DATEVALUE() (like VALUE()) fails loudly with #VALUE! on genuinely non-date text, which is a feature — it flags rows that need attention instead of guessing.

questions.q: Why does this lesson matter specifically for VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH, covered in Chapter 2?
options: These functions require an exact match, and a text '1024' will not match a numeric 1024 even though they look identical on screen
Lookup functions automatically fix data type mismatches
Lookup functions only work on text values, never numbers
Data types have no effect on lookup functions
questions.explain: Exact-match lookups compare the underlying value and type, not the on-screen appearance — a text/number mismatch is one of the most common causes of a lookup that 'should work' but returns an error.
